claims.text: NbTaTiV-like refractory high-entropy alloys can form a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The NbTaTiV-like baseline has lattice distortion caused by compositional fluctuations and differences in atomic radii.
High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in refractory high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by the degree of lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-radius mismatch through elemental substitution increases lattice distortion, whereas selecting elements of more similar size decreases it.
Lattice distortion changes the geometry of mobile <111>{110} edge-dislocation cores from straight to wavy.
Atomic-size heterogeneity produces severe local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions force edge-dislocation cores away from their neutral planes and create wavy dislocation lines.
Wavy edge-dislocation lines impede or slow dislocation glide.
Retarded dislocation glide increases strain hardening.
Increased strain hardening delays plastic instability or catastrophic failure and thereby improves elevated-temperature toughness.
Variants with greater lattice distortion will exhibit more pronounced wavy dislocation cores than the lower-distortion baseline.
Variants with greater lattice distortion will exhibit greater high-temperature strain hardening and toughness than the lower-distortion baseline.
Greater lattice distortion may improve strain hardening and toughness despite producing lower yield strength.
The NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy remains a single BCC phase up to 900°C.
The proposed mechanism should dominate in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys during deformation at 600–900°C.
The mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys or systems in which screw-dislocation-controlled plasticity prevails.
High-temperature mechanical testing of NbTaTiV-like material at temperatures within the proposed elevated-temperature regime and at a controlled strain rate is feasible.
The yield strength of NbTaTiV decreases from 1064 MPa at room temperature to 595 MPa at 900°C.
Grain-boundary effects and residual stresses may also affect high-temperature mechanical behavior.
